[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is drospirenone, a rigid lipophilic 17-spirolactone steroid; no drospirenone-specific F record is present, but the closest L4 analog spironolactone, sharing the 17-spirolactone/3-keto-4-ene core, has an experimental human fraction absorbed of 100% (C112), and canrenone, the spirolactone metabolite, produced substantial oral AUC in humans (C68, C56, C70, C82).

L4 consistently reports high human fraction absorbed for lipophilic steroids: dexamethasone 100% (C108), prednisolone 95% (C134), hydrocortisone 89–95% (C122, C152), corticosterone 100% (C145), testosterone 100% (C146, C113), progesterone 91% (C153), prednisone >95% (C155), and methylprednisolone fa 0.82 (C107).

L5 adds mechanistic gut-wall evidence: budesonide showed high bidirectional permeability with efflux ratio 1 and no P-gp efflux (C199, C157, C188, C176, C178); testosterone and hydrocortisone are high-permeability passive-transport references (C187, C191, C196, C183); progesterone transport was enhanced across Caco-2/everted sac (C198); prednisone showed rapid uptake in gut-chip (C184). These support high intestinal absorption without efflux limitation for lipophilic steroids.

Some L5 records show P-gp efflux for other steroids (prednisolone C194, estrone C156, ethynyl estradiol C166), but these are structurally less similar to drospirenone (corticosteroid/phenolic estrogens) and do not provide affirmative drospirenone-specific presystemic loss; mechanism alone is not an F result.
No affirmative threshold-relevant evidence supports F<20%; the unfavorable solubility prior is not an F measurement, and L3/L4/L5 absorption/permeability evidence supports the absorption component.

evidence_gaps: No drospirenone-specific absolute oral bioavailability record is present in any level; all F evidence comes from reference contexts and structural analogs.
No drospirenone-specific gut-wall efflux or intestinal metabolism record is present in L5; the records are for other steroids/compounds.
L5 efflux records for prednisolone, estrone, and ethynyl estradiol are low-transferability and do not establish drospirenone presystemic loss.
Query species, formulation, dose, prandial state, and disease condition are unspecified; species-dependent F remains possible.
No drospirenone-specific solubility or dissolution measurement is available; the unfavorable solubility prior is not affirmative evidence of F<20%.
L3 oral AUC records lack IV comparators and measure canrenone or co-administered hormones, not drospirenone itself.
content.decision_summary: L5 adds mechanistic gut-wall evidence that lipophilic steroids generally show high passive permeability and, for budesonide/testosterone/hydrocortisone/progesterone, no efflux limitation; the few P-gp substrate records involve structurally distant steroids and are low-transferability. Combined with L4 spironolactone 100% fraction absorbed and L3 canrenone oral exposure, F>=20% remains better supported; prediction high, moderate confidence, strengthened.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
